opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the simplest way to put it is that Ai2 is a nonprofit, and that shapes almost everything about how we work. We're not trying to ship a product or hit a revenue number. The mission is to do AI research for the common good, and in practice, for the language modeling team, that has come to mean being fully open. Not just releasing weights, but the data, the training code, the intermediate checkpoints, the evaluation setup, all of it. With OLMo and Tülu, the goal is that someone at a university or a small company could actually reproduce what we did and build on it.

Culturally, that creates a different energy than a frontier lab. We're much smaller, so people own big pieces of the pipeline. A relatively junior researcher might be responsible for the whole post-training recipe for one release, or a data mixture that goes into pretraining. There's a lot of trust, and also a lot of pressure, because you can't hide behind a huge org.

There's also a strong bias toward shipping. Even though we're a research institute, it doesn't feel like a traditional academic lab where everyone writes their own paper and moves on. It feels more like a team building one artifact together, the model, and the papers fall out of that. You get this mix of academic values, like openness and documenting everything, with more of a startup-style execution culture.

The tension, honestly, is compute and talent. We have far less compute than the big labs, so we have to be really careful about which experiments we run. That forces a kind of discipline, but it also means we're often a step behind on scale. So a lot of what we contribute is showing the community *how* things work, how RL with verifiable rewards behaves, how to do post-training well, rather than having the single biggest model.

And for me personally, the reason I'm there is that I think the world needs at least a few serious groups doing truly open frontier-ish work. If everything important happens behind closed doors, researchers lose the ability to study these systems, and policymakers lose a real reference point. Ai2 is one of the few places structured to actually do that, so the culture is very mission-driven. People are there because they believe openness matters.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about Ai2's research culture is that it's built around openness as a first principle rather than as an afterthought. A lot of labs will release a model and call it open, but what they mean is that you can download the weights. At Ai2, the bar is higher: we want to release the data, the training code, the intermediate checkpoints, the evaluation setups, and the write-ups that explain why we made the decisions we made. OLMo and Tülu are the clearest examples of that. The goal isn't just to give people an artifact, it's to let them reproduce the work and build on it.

That shapes how people operate day to day. Because we know everything is going to be public, there's less incentive to hide failures or dress up results. We publish the things that didn't work, we document the data mixes honestly, and we try to make the paper match what actually happened in training. Being a nonprofit helps with that. We don't have to protect a product moat, so the question is never "what gives us an edge," it's "what helps the field understand how these models actually get built."

The other piece is that Ai2 sits somewhere between academia and an industrial lab. We have the compute and engineering to train real frontier-adjacent models, which most universities can't do, but we also have the academic habits of writing things down carefully, releasing them, and engaging with the broader community. That combination is rare, and I think it's why people come to Ai2. It's a place where you can do serious large-scale work and still have it be fully open.

There are tradeoffs. Openness is slower, and you spend a lot of time on documentation and cleanup that a closed lab would skip. We also can't match the compute of the biggest companies, so we have to be strategic about which problems we pick. But I think the bet is that the ecosystem needs at least one well-resourced lab whose whole mission is showing the recipe, and that's the culture we're trying to sustain.

astra-6.text:
I think of Ai2 as a place where the research itself is the center of gravity. There’s room to ask longer-term questions, and success isn’t just about getting a capability into a product. It’s also about whether we learned something useful and whether other people can build on it.

For me, openness is a big part of that culture. With language models, publishing a paper or releasing weights only tells part of the story. The data, the training process, the things you tried that didn’t work—those are often what another researcher needs to actually understand the result. Making that work accessible takes effort, but it makes the research more valuable.

And there’s an interesting tension there: you want to move quickly and build strong models, but you also want to be careful about what you’re claiming. I see those as complementary ambitions. Building something competitive gives you a much better foundation for studying how it works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Ai2’s research culture is built around openness and giving researchers room to pursue questions they think matter. There’s an emphasis on doing strong scientific work, but also on making that work useful to people outside the institute. That means sharing enough of the process that other researchers can understand it, challenge it, and build on it.

For me, those two things reinforce each other. When you work openly, you have to be clear about what you’ve learned, what didn’t work, and what you still don’t understand. And having the freedom to investigate those questions makes the research more interesting.
